summary: Analyzes issues in moving unmanaged networks, such as home and small office networks, from IPv4 to IPv6. It examines transition mechanisms against the needs of these networks, which have no professional administrator.

plainLanguage.summary: Home networks have no expert on staff. This document looks at which ways of switching to the new address system work for them.

questions: evaluating ipv6 transition mechanisms for small offices
how do home networks transition to ipv6
subtitle: Evaluating how to move home networks from IPv4 to IPv6.

tldr.problem: Home networks and small offices have no dedicated IT staff. They need to transition from IPv4 to IPv6, but existing mechanisms differ in how they handle NAT, require configuration, and affect network performance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC evaluates four deployment scenarios and analyzes tunneling solutions along two dimensions: whether they are automatic or require configuration, and whether they can traverse NAT boxes. It recommends developing four types of solutions to cover all cases.
tldr.outcome: The analysis shows that different deployment scenarios require different mechanisms. Isolated hosts benefit from automatic tunnels, while networks with ISP support work better with configured tunnels.

sections.title: Home Networks Transitioning to IPv6
sections.content:
Unmanaged networks are home networks and small office networks that have no professional IT staff to manage them. Unlike enterprise networks, these networks cannot rely on skilled administrators to configure complex transition mechanisms. The RFC analyzes what mechanisms allow these networks to gain IPv6 connectivity while maintaining the simplicity they require.

Four deployment scenarios guide the analysis. In scenario A, an isolated host gains global IPv6 connectivity to reach the Internet; scenario B assumes both the gateway and ISP are dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6); scenario C has an IPv4-only ISP; and scenario D has an IPv6-only ISP. Each scenario presents different challenges and requires different solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Home networks need to switch to a new address system but have no IT staff. This memo looks at four different situations homes might find themselves in and what works best for each one.

sections.title: Two Dimensions of Tunneling Solutions
sections.content:
When a network cannot obtain native IPv6 service from its Internet Service Provider, it must tunnel IPv6 packets over the existing IPv4 network. The RFC classifies tunneling solutions along two key dimensions.

The first dimension is deployment automation. Automatic solutions like 6to4 and Teredo work with minimal setup: a host derives its IPv6 address from its IPv4 address or by negotiating with a server, without requiring explicit configuration. Configured solutions like tunnel brokers require the network to explicitly identify a tunnel server and set up the tunnel before use.

The second dimension is NAT traversal. Some networks sit behind a Network Address Translator, which converts between local private addresses and a public Internet address. Tunneling mechanisms designed for NAT traversal encapsulate packets inside UDP or TCP, which most NATs allow, while simpler mechanisms use direct IPv4 encapsulation (protocol 41), which many NATs block.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunneling is like putting a letter inside an envelope to send it. Some envelopes (automatic) require no work from you; others (configured) need you to pick which mailbox to use. Some envelopes get through home routers easily; others get stuck.

sections.title: Trade-offs Between Automatic and Configured Approaches
sections.content:
Configured tunnels offer strong advantages. A host obtains a stable IPv6 address that persists across IPv4 address changes. The service provider is accountable for quality and can support multicast packets. Reverse DNS lookups work reliably. However, configured tunnels require explicit setup and, if operated by a third party, concentrate traffic through the tunnel server, increasing costs for the operator.

Automatic tunnels require no setup and can optimize traffic paths: two automatic-tunnel hosts exchange data directly using their underlying IPv4 connectivity instead of routing through a central server. However, the IPv6 address stability depends on IPv4 address stability, and relays operated by third parties incur costs. A key risk is the emergence of parallel IPv6 internets: if 6to4 hosts cannot reach native IPv6 hosts without going through a gateway, both technologies fragment the global IPv6 space.

Both approaches have roles. The RFC recommends developing both automatic tunnels (for cost-effective deployment) and configured tunnels (for stable service when ISPs provide them).
sections.plainLanguage: Quick methods (automatic) work without help from anyone, but addresses change every time your home network restarts. Set-up methods (configured) keep your address stable and someone cares about service quality, but they need planning. The best internet has both.

sections.title: Four Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Scenario A: Isolated Host. A single IPv6-capable host needs global connectivity but the gateway does not support IPv6. Automatic tunneling mechanisms like Teredo fit this case well, as they require no ISP involvement and work through NAT.

Scenario B: Dual-Stack Gateway and ISP. Both the local gateway and the ISP support both IPv4 and IPv6. The main task is prefix delegation: the ISP gives the gateway an IPv6 prefix to distribute to its local hosts. This can be done via explicit DHCPv6 prefix delegation or by extending a /64 prefix across multiple links using neighbor discovery proxies. Name resolution (DNS) must be provisioned to allow hosts to find IPv6 addresses of remote services and publish their own addresses locally.

Scenario C: IPv4-Only ISP. The gateway is dual-stack but the ISP provides only IPv4. Automatic tunneling via 6to4 allows the gateway to connect to the IPv6 Internet through relay routers. Configured tunnels are an alternative if the ISP is willing to provide them.

Scenario D: IPv6-Only ISP. The gateway receives only IPv6 from the ISP. Local hosts that still need IPv4 connectivity must use IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling, a mechanism that has received little IETF standardization effort but is needed for transition.
sections.plainLanguage: Isolated host: you're alone needing IPv6; use automatic tunneling. Dual-stack ISP: the easiest case; give each host an address from the ISP's range. IPv4-only ISP: use relay routers. IPv6-only ISP: hosts needing IPv4 must tunnel backwards, a case few tools support yet.

sections.title: Security Implications of IPv6 Transition
sections.content:
Transition mechanisms raise new security challenges. When a host behind a NAT gains direct IPv6 connectivity, it loses the implicit filtering that NAT provided. Unless developers restrict applications, services running on the host may become accessible to the entire IPv6 Internet, exposing them to new attack vectors.

Relay-based solutions introduce new risks: improperly designed relays or protocols could enable attacks on Internet services. Transition mechanisms that involve third-party infrastructure (such as public relay services) create dependencies on the reliability and security of those relays. Default firewalling policies must carefully balance security with usability, allowing applications designed for global connectivity while restricting local services to local networks.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT used to act like a bouncer at a door: the Internet could not knock, so services stayed hidden. IPv6 opens the door. Now you need a firewall that only lets in visitors your services invited. Third-party relays are like hiring a shipping company; you must trust them.
